description: Focus indicators for actionable elements must be present and meet contrast requirements.
recommendedFix:
A focus indicator must always be visible and have at least 3:1 contrast.

It is best to intentionally style the focus indicator for all links, buttons, fields, etc. We encourage you to change the shape somehow (add a border, box, underline, etc.) as well as choose a color that has sufficient contrast with either the background of the page (if placed outside of the element) or the element itself (if placed inside of the element).

description: Errors are not identified to screen reader users.
recommendedFix:
Ensure that screen reader users are informed of the errors present for these form fields.

There are a number of ways that this can be addressed. Ideally, add an `aria-describedby` attribute and set focus on the first form field with an error. The `aria-describedby` attribute should be placed on the affected form field. It takes the `ID` of the element that contains the description of the error. If the form field is described by more than one element, you can set the `aria-describedby` attribute to a space-separated list of IDs.

Some alternative approaches are the following:

* Add an `aria-invalid` attribute to the `<input>` elements with errors. Ideally this is accompanied by setting focus on the first `<input>` with an error.
* Utilize the browser error alerts to indicate this information.

description: Decorative SVG elements should be hidden from screen reader users.

description: Content that functions as a list should be indicated as such to screen reader users.

description: Text that functions as a heading should be marked up as such.
recommendedFix:
Mark this text up as a heading.

- An `<h2>` should head each major section of the page.
- Subsequent heading levels (`<h3>` through `<h6>`) should be related to a parent `<h2>` and should not skip heading levels.

Please see the section regarding [Tooltip that is only available on smaller viewports](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/524#heading-tooltip-that-is-only-available-on-smaller-viewports) for more information on mobile responsive tooltips and a code sample illustrating this functionality.

Once you have decided which type of tooltip to implement (manual or automatic), please make a comment on this issue to let us know, and then include this issue in an upcoming QA or reach out to your CSM to have this content audited. description: The modal dialog container is not labeled.
recommendedFix:
Provide a [label using one of the following methods](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/820#heading-labelling). All of these solutions are acceptable, but some may be easier to implement than others depending on the content within the modal dialog.

1. Add a heading (preferably an `<h1>`, but `<h2>` is acceptable), then associate it with the modal dialog wrapper by giving that heading a unique `id` and referencing it with an `aria-labelledby` attribute on the wrapper element (the element with `role="dialog"` and `aria-modal="true"`).
  * If a heading describing the contents of the modal dialog already exists, you can use that heading instead.
  * This heading is most helpful when it is visible for all users, but for strict WCAG conformance it can be made visible only to screen reader users instead.
1. Alternatively, add an `aria-label` attribute to the wrapper element (the element with `role="dialog"` and `aria-modal="true"`) describing the purpose of the modal dialog.

description: This live filter region requires additional ARIA markup to assist screen reader users in understanding what this section is for, and where it begins and ends.
recommendedFix:
Wrap both the text field and the content that it filters in a `<section>` tag or a `<div>` with `role=“region”` so that screen reader users can tell that they are related. 

Give this wrapper element a generic `aria-label` attribute value that broadly identifies what kind of content is being filtered. For example, “location filter” or “product filter”. 

See the [wrapper markup section](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/922#heading-wrapper) of the Knowledge Base article on Live Filters.

description: Screen Reader only text must be provided to describe the relationship between the live filter and its content.
recommendedFix:
Add screen reader only text inside of the filter region and before the input that provides instructions on how to use this live filter. 

For example, "The following text field filters the results that follow as you type."  Extend this screen reader only statement with additional instruction text tailored to your content and functionality.

description: Content changes are not announced as users enter text in the live filter input.
recommendedFix: Use a “live region” to announce when the filtered content changes as the user types in the text field. To accomplish this, add a visually hidden container, and give this container the `aria-live=”assertive”` attribute. When results are found, insert text into this container similar to "[#] results available". When no results are found, insert text like "no results available" so that users know that they should probably stop typing and try a different search term.

description: Keyboard users are unable to interact with these tabs as expected.
recommendedFix:
Keyboard and screen reader users will expect to be able to interact with these tabs in the following ways:

1. Only the currently selected tab should be focusable via the tab key. To do this, add a `tabindex="-1"` to all non-selected tabs.
1. Ensure that the `Left` and `Right` arrow keys allow the user to traverse the options in the tablist.
1. Tabs can be activated automatically or manually. If they are activated automatically, the tabs will be selected as they are traversed via the arrow keys. If they are activated manually, they will be selected by pressing either the `Enter` or `Space` key. Ensure that the `aria-selected` and `tabindex` attributes are updated as the new tab is activated. See this [section about automatic versus manual activation](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/606#heading-automatic-versus-manual-tab-activation) in the related Knowledge Base article to learn more.

If these tabs are arranged vertically, ensure that users can use the `Up` and `Down` arrow keys (in addition to `Left` and `Right`) to traverse the tabs.

Optionally, you may additionally choose to allow users to use the `Home` and `End` keys to navigate to the start and end of the tablist.

description: Keyboard and screen reader users do not have their focus moved to this modal dialog when it opens.
recommendedFix:
Set the keyboard focus to the [most appropriate element](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/820#heading-moving-focus-into-a-modal-dialog-when-it-opens) inside this modal dialog, depending on the content it contains. All of the following solutions are acceptable, and you are free to decide which solution feels the most "appropriate" to you in this use case.

1. To the close (X) button, if one is used.
1. To the visible heading that labels the modal dialog, if one is used.
1. To the modal dialog wrapper itself (the element with both `role="dialog"` and `aria-modal="true"`).
1. To the primary call to action (CTA) element (such as an "OK" button), or the element for the least destructive action in a set of CTAs (like "Cancel" next to a button for "Delete").

**Note:** in order to set focus on an element that cannot natively receive focus (like a heading or the wrapper element), add the attribute `tabindex="-1"` to it.

description: Keyboard users are able to focus on elements outside of this modal dialog while it is open.

description: Closing this modal dialog does not return the user to the element that opened it.

description: This modal dialog is missing necessary ARIA attributes.

Do not [add these attributes](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/820#heading--do-not-dynamically-add-these-attributes-while-a-users-focus-is-inside) dynamically after the user's focus has been moved to it or into it.

description: This is a button, but it is not marked up as such; screen readers will not identify it as actionable and it will not be usable by keyboard users.
recommendedFix:

description: This color combination does not meet the minimum color contrast required by the WCAG. The combination of gray (#D0D0D7) and white (#FFFFFF) only has a contrast ratio of 1.47:1.

description: Text that functions as a heading should be marked up as such.

description: All form fields must be properly labeled.

description: Checkbox sets must have a fieldset and legend.

description: This page contains one or more heading levels in an illogical order.
recommendedFix:

description: Undersized targets cause problems for some users.
recommendedFix:
Users with reduced fine motor skills may have difficulty selecting smaller target areas, or may accidentally select another target nearby.  

Ensure pointer targets are large enough to allow for a 24 px square to be placed inside of it.

If this is not possible, provide sufficient space between targets: 

* at least 24 px between the center point of the undersized target and the center point of any other undersized target
* at least 12 px between the center point of the undersized target and the edge of a sufficiently sized target.

See the [WCAG Guideline](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/target-size-minimum.html) for more guidance on target size and spacing.

description: These tab controls are missing critical ARIA attributes.

* Add the attribute `aria-labelledby` to the element with `role=”tabpanel”` and set its value equal to the `id` of the tab element that controls it.
* Optionally, as a usability best practice, add `tabindex="0"` to each tab panel to make the component easier for inexperienced keyboard-only users to navigate.

description: Keyboard users are unable to interact with these tabs as expected.
recommendedFix:

1. Ensure that the `Left` and `Right` arrow keys allow the user to traverse the options in the tablist.
1. Tabs can be activated automatically or manually. If they are activated automatically, the tabs will be selected as they are traversed via the arrow keys. If they are activated manually, they will be selected by pressing either the `Enter` or `Space` key. Ensure that the `aria-selected` and `tabindex` attributes are updated as the new tab is activated. See this [section about automatic versus manual activation](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/606#heading-automatic-versus-manual-tab-activation) in the related Knowledge Base article to learn more.

If these tabs are arranged vertically, ensure that users can use the `Up` and `Down` arrow keys (in addition to `Left` and `Right`) to traverse the tabs.

Optionally, you may additionally choose to allow users to use the `Home` and `End` keys to navigate to the start and end of the tablist.

description: Focus indicators for actionable elements must be present and meet contrast requirements.
recommendedFix:
A focus indicator must always be visible and have at least 3:1 contrast.

It is best to intentionally style the focus indicator for all links, buttons, fields, etc. We encourage you to change the shape somehow (add a border, box, underline, etc.) as well as choose a color that has sufficient contrast with either the background of the page (if placed outside of the element) or the element itself (if placed inside of the element).

description: All form fields must be properly labeled.
recommendedFix: Ensure all form fields have a visible label (typically via a `<label>` tag) which is properly associated with its field (via the `for` attribute, which takes the value of the `id` from the form field).

description: Text that functions as a heading should be marked up as such.
recommendedFix:
Mark this text up as a heading.

Headings provide structure for screen reader users. When marking text up as a heading, verify that the page maintains a logical outline structure. For example; 

- Each page needs a single `<h1>` heading that describes the main purpose of the page.
- An `<h2>` should head each major section of the page.
- Subsequent heading levels (`<h3>` through `<h6>`) should be related to a parent `<h2>` and should not skip heading levels.

description: Text within images causes problems for screen reader users and users of magnification technology.
recommendedFix:
**Preferred Remediation:**

- Extract the text from the image and place it on the page using HTML; use CSS to style and position it as desired superimposed over the image(s).
_Or…_
- Place the text on the page adjacent to the image, similar to a caption.

**Alternative Remediation:**

We recognize solving this issue using the preferred method may not be feasible for all situations, so completing all of the numbered steps is an alternative solution to close this issue: 

1. Add all of the text from the image, and [any other visual information necessary for understanding](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/472), to an `alt` attribute on the image. If the `alt` attribute is already present, ensure it accurately reflects the text within the image and that the other steps for this recommendation are followed.
1. Ensure that the image is reasonably readable up to 200% zoom.
1. (Optional) Add only the text from the image as a title attribute to the image to assist magnification users.

**Reminder:** When overlaying text on an image, make sure the [text has proper contrast](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/862#heading-text-over-images-and-complex-backgrounds) to the background image. 

Please note, this method will not meet WCAG 1.4.5, but it has been determined to be an acceptable exception to resolve this issue. **By choosing the “Alternative Remediation” method described above you are accepting any accessibility liability risk for this content and understand that this remediation option does not comply with the associated WCAG guidelines which will continue to present some accessibility issues.**

After this alternative remediation has been successfully implemented, we will downgrade this issue to a warning (P3) with a comment indicating as such and set the issue status to Not Fixing. This status will not prevent you from obtaining a Letter of Conformance and it is encouraged that you attempt to fully remediate this content using the preferred remediation methods during future updates.

description: Images that lack alt attributes make it impossible for screen reader users to know what the image depicts.
recommendedFix:
Ensure each image has an `alt` attribute. The content of the alt attribute depends on the image type.

If an image is **informative** (i.e. provides information not conveyed in other ways), add an `alt` attribute to the image which conveys the information provided by it.
If an image is **decorative** (i.e. does not contribute any meaningful information), give the image an empty `alt` attribute (`alt=“”`).

For more advice on determining which images are decorative or informative, visit our Knowledge Base Article: [The Art of Alt Attributes](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/472).

description: Form field groupings must have a fieldset and legend.
recommendedFix: Wrap each set of form fields in a `fieldset` and wrap the text labeling the form fields in a `<legend>` tag. Ensure that the `<legend>` tag is the first child of the `fieldset` it labels.

affectedItem: "Search in" and "Sort View" set of radio buttons
description: Radio button sets must have fieldsets and legends.
recommendedFix:
Wrap each radio button set in a fieldset and wrap the text labeling each set of radio buttons in a `<legend>` tag. Ensure that the `<legend>` tag is the first child of the `<fieldset>` that it labels.

If this radio button set has been [created using custom elements](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/525#heading-checkboxes-and-radio-buttons-with-custom-elements) and ARIA, it will be necessary to use `role="radiogroup"` and `aria-label`/`aria-labelledby` attributes instead.

description: When an asterisk is used as a symbol, but the meaning of the symbol is not defined, it can cause confusion for some users.
recommendedFix: Define the meaning of the asterisks at the start of the form. For example, add text that says: "* indicates a required field" or similar.

description: Instructions that are not programmatically associated with their relevant form fields may not be available to screen reader users.
recommendedFix: Associate the instructions with their relevant form fields via the `aria-describedby` attribute. The `aria-describedby` attribute should be placed on the relevant form field, and should be assigned the `id` of the instructions to be associated. If the field is described by more than one element, you can set the `aria-describedby` attribute to a space separated list of `id` values.

description: Form fields that are required must be programmatically indicated to screen reader users.
recommendedFix: Preferably, the `required` attribute should be used or less preferred, use an `aria-required` attribute.

description: Errors are not identified to screen reader users.
recommendedFix:
Ensure that screen reader users are informed of the errors present for these form fields.

There are a number of ways that this can be addressed. Ideally, add an `aria-describedby` attribute and set focus on the first form field with an error. The `aria-describedby` attribute should be placed on the affected form field. It takes the `ID` of the element that contains the description of the error. If the form field is described by more than one element, you can set the `aria-describedby` attribute to a space-separated list of IDs.

Some alternative approaches are the following:

* Add an `aria-invalid` attribute to the `<input>` elements with errors. Ideally this is accompanied by setting focus on the first `<input>` with an error.
* Utilize the browser error alerts to indicate this information.

description: Tooltip content must be reachable by all users, including screen reader and keyboard users.
recommendedFix:
Making tooltips accessible can be accomplished in two distinct ways:

- Make your tooltips accessible by using **manually**-activated tooltips. Please see [this section](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/524#heading-for-manuallyactivated-tooltips) in the Tooltips Knowledge Base article.
- Make your tooltips accessible by using **automatically**-activated tooltips. Please see [this section](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/524#heading-for-automaticallyactivated-tooltips) in the Tooltips Knowledge Base article.
  - **Note:** If you elect to use automatically-activated tooltips, these tooltips must convert to manually-activated tooltips when they are displayed on smaller viewports with a responsive layout. Please see the section regarding [Tooltip that is only available on smaller viewports](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/524#heading-tooltip-that-is-only-available-on-smaller-viewports) for more information on mobile responsive tooltips and a code sample illustrating this functionality.

Once you have decided which type of tooltip to implement (manual or automatic), please make a comment on this issue to let us know, and then include this issue in an upcoming QA or reach out to your CSM to have this content audited. We will then set this issue to Not Applicable and add new issues as needed to address the content.

description: Elements that are marked up as buttons but function as links can cause confusion for screen reader users.
recommendedFix: Mark each element up as a link. Alternatively, give each element a `role="link"` attribute.

description: Focus indicators for actionable elements must be present and meet contrast requirements.
recommendedFix:
A focus indicator must always be visible and have at least 3:1 contrast.

It is best to intentionally style the focus indicator for all links, buttons, fields, etc. We encourage you to change the shape somehow (add a border, box, underline, etc.) as well as choose a color that has sufficient contrast with either the background of the page (if placed outside of the element) or the element itself (if placed inside of the element).

description: Text that functions as a heading should be marked up as such.
recommendedFix:
Mark this text up as a heading.

Headings provide structure for screen reader users. When marking text up as a heading, verify that the page maintains a logical outline structure. For example; 

- Each page needs a single `<h1>` heading that describes the main purpose of the page.
- An `<h2>` should head each major section of the page.
- Subsequent heading levels (`<h3>` through `<h6>`) should be related to a parent `<h2>` and should not skip heading levels.

description: All form fields must be properly labeled.
recommendedFix: Ensure all form fields have a visible label (typically via a `<label>` tag) which is properly associated with its field (via the `for` attribute, which takes the value of the `id` from the form field).

description: Radio button sets must have fieldsets and legends.
recommendedFix:
Wrap each radio button set in a fieldset and wrap the text labeling each set of radio buttons in a `<legend>` tag. Ensure that the `<legend>` tag is the first child of the `<fieldset>` that it labels.

If this radio button set has been [created using custom elements](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/525#heading-checkboxes-and-radio-buttons-with-custom-elements) and ARIA, it will be necessary to use `role="radiogroup"` and `aria-label`/`aria-labelledby` attributes instead.

description: When content is marked up as a table, but is not semantically a table, it can be confusing for screen reader users.
recommendedFix:
Preferably remove the `<table>` wrapping this content.

Less preferably, add the attribute `role="presentation"` to the `<table>` tag. Ensure that the content is responsive so that it does not require horizontal scrolling.

description: Telephone numbers should be marked up as links.

description: Form fields that are required must be programmatically indicated to screen reader users.
recommendedFix: Preferably, the `required` attribute should be used or less preferred, use an `aria-required` attribute.

description: Elements that are marked up as links but function as buttons can cause confusion for screen reader users.
recommendedFix:
Mark each element up as a `<button>`. 

Alternatively, ensure that custom button elements include `role="button”` and `tabindex=“0”`, and have the appropriate scripting in place so that the element can be selected by keyboard users using the `Enter` key and `Space` key, and by mouse click.

description: Elements that control expandable content must be indicated to screen reader users.
recommendedFix: Add an `aria-controls` attribute to each element that controls expandable content and set the value of that attribute to equal the `id` of the tag that wraps the expanded content. Also add an `aria-expanded="true"` attribute to that same control element when content is expanded, and `aria-expanded="false"` otherwise.

description: Calendar / datepicker popups may present challenges to keyboard and screen reader users, but this is mitigated when users can still enter a date using the associated text field.
recommendedFix: Since a mechanism is available for screen reader and keyboard users to enter a date, this functionality can be used by disabled users. However, we would encourage you to investigate the possibility of making the datepicker accessible as well to provide a more equivalent experience. See the associated article for more details on how to accomplish this.

description: This complex content requires a consultation.
recommendedFix:
Due to the complex nature and functionality of this content, a consultation call will be necessary to determine the best approach to making this accessible.

The main accessibility issue is that keyboard and screen reader users are unable to trigger the view that mouse users can when double clicking on the fields. 

Please reach out to your Allyant Customer Success Manager to set up a consultation to discuss remediation options.

description: Images that lack alt attributes make it impossible for screen reader users to know what the image depicts.
recommendedFix:
Ensure each image has an `alt` attribute. The content of the alt attribute depends on the image type.

If an image is **informative** (i.e. provides information not conveyed in other ways), add an `alt` attribute to the image which conveys the information provided by it.
If an image is **decorative** (i.e. does not contribute any meaningful information), give the image an empty `alt` attribute (`alt=“”`).

For more advice on determining which images are decorative or informative, visit our Knowledge Base Article: [The Art of Alt Attributes](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/472).

description: Tooltip content must be reachable by all users, including screen reader and keyboard users.
recommendedFix:
Making tooltips accessible can be accomplished in two distinct ways:

- Make your tooltips accessible by using **manually**-activated tooltips. Please see [this section](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/524#heading-for-manuallyactivated-tooltips) in the Tooltips Knowledge Base article.
- Make your tooltips accessible by using **automatically**-activated tooltips. Please see [this section](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/524#heading-for-automaticallyactivated-tooltips) in the Tooltips Knowledge Base article.
  - **Note:** If you elect to use automatically-activated tooltips, these tooltips must convert to manually-activated tooltips when they are displayed on smaller viewports with a responsive layout. Please see the section regarding [Tooltip that is only available on smaller viewports](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/524#heading-tooltip-that-is-only-available-on-smaller-viewports) for more information on mobile responsive tooltips and a code sample illustrating this functionality.

Once you have decided which type of tooltip to implement (manual or automatic), please make a comment on this issue to let us know, and then include this issue in an upcoming QA or reach out to your CSM to have this content audited. We will then set this issue to Not Applicable and add new issues as needed to address the content.

Ensure that text serving as the header for each row (if present) is wrapped in a `<th scope=“row”>`. Often this text is the first cell in each row, [but not always](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/29#heading-not-always-the-first-row-or-first-column).

description: This color combination does not meet the minimum color contrast required by the WCAG. The combination of blue (#217CBB) and light blue (#DCEDF9) only has a contrast ratio of 3.75:1.
recommendedFix:
The visual presentation of all instances of text & images of text presented in this color combination — across the entire site — should be modified to have a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1. Larger text with a size of at least 18pt (24px or 1.5em), or 14pt (18.66px or 1.2em) and bold (font-weight: 700 or more), only requires a minimum contrast ratio of 3:1.

**Note:** the color combination specified in this issue’s example may also be present elsewhere on your site. We recommend careful review and monitoring of all site colors to ensure ongoing, site wide compliance with color contrast requirements.

description: Elements that are marked up as buttons but function as links can cause confusion for screen reader users.
recommendedFix: Mark each element up as a link. Alternatively, give each element a `role="link"` attribute.

description: The modal dialog container is not labeled.
recommendedFix:
Provide a [label using one of the following methods](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/820#heading-labelling). All of these solutions are acceptable, but some may be easier to implement than others depending on the content within the modal dialog.

1. Add a heading (preferably an `<h1>`, but `<h2>` is acceptable), then associate it with the modal dialog wrapper by giving that heading a unique `id` and referencing it with an `aria-labelledby` attribute on the wrapper element (the element with `role="dialog"` and `aria-modal="true"`).
  * If a heading describing the contents of the modal dialog already exists, you can use that heading instead.
  * This heading is most helpful when it is visible for all users, but for strict WCAG conformance it can be made visible only to screen reader users instead.
1. Alternatively, add an `aria-label` attribute to the wrapper element (the element with `role="dialog"` and `aria-modal="true"`) describing the purpose of the modal dialog.

description: This modal dialog is missing necessary ARIA attributes.
recommendedFix: Ensure the attributes `role="dialog"` and `aria-modal="true"` are present on the wrapper element of this modal dialog. Do not [add these attributes](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/820#heading--do-not-dynamically-add-these-attributes-while-a-users-focus-is-inside) dynamically after the user's focus has been moved to it or into it.

description: Unnecessary ARIA attributes can cause unexpected behavior for screen reader users.
recommendedFix: The presence of an unnecessary ARIA attribute can create unexpected behavior across various configurations. Remove the `aria-pressed` attribute from the element.

description: Existing label elements should be programmatically associated with their form fields.
recommendedFix: Ensure each `<label>` tag is assigned a `for` attribute whose value matches the `id` of the form it is meant to label.

description: This autocomplete lacks instructions for screen reader users.
recommendedFix:
Add clear, succinct instructions as screen-reader-only text, then associate them with the input field using the `aria-describedby` attribute. See the [section about instructions](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/427#heading-instructions-for-screen-reader-users) in the Autocompletes Knowledge Base article for more information.

For the best user experience possible, conditionally add `aria-hidden="true"` to this text element when the input field is not focused so that screen reader users won't encounter it as they navigate the page.

description: These autocomplete results are missing critical ARIA attributes.
recommendedFix:
Add `role="listbox"` to the `<ul>` containing the results. Add an `aria-labelledby` attribute to the `<ul>`. The `aria-labelledby` attribute takes the ID of the `<label>` associated with the autocomplete's text input field.

Next, add `role="option"` to each `<li>`. Ensure that each of these list items has a unique `id` attribute value.

See [this section](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/427#heading-simple-listbox-popup) of the Autocompletes Knowledge Base article for additional guidance.

description: This text input with autocomplete functionality is missing critical ARIA attributes.
recommendedFix:
Add an `aria-autocomplete` attribute. Set the value of the attribute to `list` if displaying a list of options; set the value to `inline` if displaying a single autocomplete option within the input field; or set the value to `both` if using a combination.

Additionally, if a list popup is used:

1. Add `aria-controls="[ID of list element]"`.
1. Add `aria-haspopup="listbox"`.
1. Add `aria-expanded` and set its value to `true` or `false` based on the visibility of the list. Update this value as necessary as the user interacts with the autocomplete.

See [this section of the Autocompletes KB article](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/427#heading-text-input) for complete guidance on marking up this text input as an autocomplete.

description: The number of autocomplete results available is not announced to screen reader users.
recommendedFix:
Ensure that the current number of available results is read out to screen reader users. Follow [the guidance in this section of the Autocompletes KB article](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/427#heading-results-found-announcements-for-screen-reader-users) for how to make this information available for screen reader users. 

Additionally, refer to the [Listbox Popup code sample](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/427#heading-listbox-popup).

description: When an element is activated that causes content on the page to change, screen reader users should be informed of this change.
recommendedFix:
Add screen reader only warning text before the element that says, "Activating this element will cause content on the page to be updated.".

If more than one element causes the page to update, place only one instance of the screen reader only warning text directly before the elements so that this text is not overly verbose for screen reader users.

description: SVG elements depicting important information need to be properly labeled.
recommendedFix:
Add `role="img"` and `aria-labelledby` attributes to each `<svg>` tag, then add a `<title>` tag within the `<svg>` tag and give this `<title>` tag a unique `id` attribute. Ensure the `<title>` is a direct descendant of the `<svg>` tag and that the `<svg>` tag’s `aria-labelledby` attribute holds the `<title>` tag’s `id` value.
			
Alternatively, give the `<svg>` tag `role=”img”` and `aria-label` attributes. Ensure the `aria-label` accurately and concisely describes the content of each image.

description: Tooltip content must be reachable by all users, including screen reader and keyboard users.
recommendedFix:
Making tooltips accessible can be accomplished in two distinct ways:

- Make your tooltips accessible by using **manually**-activated tooltips. Please see [this section](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/524#heading-for-manuallyactivated-tooltips) in the Tooltips Knowledge Base article.
- Make your tooltips accessible by using **automatically**-activated tooltips. Please see [this section](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/524#heading-for-automaticallyactivated-tooltips) in the Tooltips Knowledge Base article.
  - **Note:** If you elect to use automatically-activated tooltips, these tooltips must convert to manually-activated tooltips when they are displayed on smaller viewports with a responsive layout. Please see the section regarding [Tooltip that is only available on smaller viewports](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/524#heading-tooltip-that-is-only-available-on-smaller-viewports) for more information on mobile responsive tooltips and a code sample illustrating this functionality.

Once you have decided which type of tooltip to implement (manual or automatic), please make a comment on this issue to let us know, and then include this issue in an upcoming QA or reach out to your CSM to have this content audited. We will then set this issue to Not Applicable and add new issues as needed to address the content.

description: When content is marked up as a table, but is not semantically a table, it can be confusing for screen reader users.
recommendedFix:
Preferably remove the `<table>` wrapping this content.

Less preferably, add the attribute `role="presentation"` to the `<table>` tag. Ensure that the content is responsive so that it does not require horizontal scrolling.

description: All form fields must be properly labeled.
recommendedFix: Ensure all form fields have a visible label (typically via a `<label>` tag) which is properly associated with its field (via the `for` attribute, which takes the value of the `id` from the form field).

description: The tabs in this tabset are not wrapped in a tablist.
recommendedFix: Wrap these tabs in an element with the attribute `role="tablist"`.

description: These tab controls are missing critical ARIA attributes.
recommendedFix:
* Add `role="tab"` to the triggering elements. 
* Add an `aria-controls` attribute to each element with the `role="tab"`. Ensure that the value of the `aria-controls` attribute is the `id` of the tabpanel it is intended to control.
* Add an `aria-selected` attribute to each of these elements as well. Set its value to "true" on the tab element that is currently active, and "false" for all other tabs. Ensure the value of this attribute is dynamically updated as the user interacts with the tabs to indicate the active tab at all times.

description: These tab panels are missing critical ARIA attributes.
recommendedFix:
* Add `role="tabpanel"` to the container element wrapping the content controlled by the related element with `role=”tab”`.
* Add the attribute `aria-labelledby` to the element with `role=”tabpanel”` and set its value equal to the `id` of the tab element that controls it.
* Optionally, as a usability best practice, add `tabindex="0"` to each tab panel to make the component easier for inexperienced keyboard-only users to navigate.

description: Keyboard users are unable to interact with these tabs as expected.
recommendedFix:
Keyboard and screen reader users will expect to be able to interact with these tabs in the following ways:

1. Only the currently selected tab should be focusable via the tab key. To do this, add a `tabindex="-1"` to all non-selected tabs.
1. Ensure that the `Left` and `Right` arrow keys allow the user to traverse the options in the tablist.
1. Tabs can be activated automatically or manually. If they are activated automatically, the tabs will be selected as they are traversed via the arrow keys. If they are activated manually, they will be selected by pressing either the `Enter` or `Space` key. Ensure that the `aria-selected` and `tabindex` attributes are updated as the new tab is activated. See this [section about automatic versus manual activation](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/606#heading-automatic-versus-manual-tab-activation) in the related Knowledge Base article to learn more.

If these tabs are arranged vertically, ensure that users can use the `Up` and `Down` arrow keys (in addition to `Left` and `Right`) to traverse the tabs.

Optionally, you may additionally choose to allow users to use the `Home` and `End` keys to navigate to the start and end of the tablist.

description: When a custom radio button or checkbox is visually hidden using the incorrect method, it is inaccessible to keyboard and screen reader users.
recommendedFix:
When custom radio buttons or checkboxes have been visually hidden using `display: none;` or `visibility: hidden;`, they are not reachable by keyboard and screen reader users. Instead, hide these `<input>` elements visually using the same techniques as described in our [Knowledge Base article on Screen Reader Only Text](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/1178).   

Note: each custom checkbox and radio button must have a `<label>` element whose `for` attribute matches the `id` of the related `<input>`. [Learn more about creating successful custom checkboxes and radio buttons.](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/525)

description: Closing this modal dialog does not return the user to the element that opened it.
recommendedFix:
When this modal dialog closes, return focus to the element that triggered this modal dialog to open.

If this element is no longer available on the page, then focus should be moved to another element as close as possible to where that element was.

If this modal dialog was opened automatically when the page loaded, then move focus on to the `<body>` element.

description: When a table column can be sorted, this must be indicated to screen reader users.

If the column is unsorted, remove the attribute, as the `aria-sort` attribute should exist on only one table header at a time.

description: Errors are not identified to screen reader users.

description: Elements that are marked up as links but function as buttons can cause confusion for screen reader users.

description: Elements that function as buttons must be marked up as such so that screen reader users will identify them as actionable and they will be usable by keyboard users.
recommendedFix:

description: Buttons must have sufficient labels for all users.

description: Elements that control expandable content must be indicated to screen reader users.

description: This element receives focus in an illogical order for screen reader and keyboard users.

description: Images that lack alt attributes make it impossible for screen reader users to know what the image depicts.
recommendedFix:

If an image is **informative** (i.e. provides information not conveyed in other ways), add an `alt` attribute to the image which conveys the information provided by it.

description: When content is marked up as a table, but is not semantically a table, it can be confusing for screen reader users.

description: Text that functions as a heading should be marked up as such.
recommendedFix:

description: Keyboard users are not able to scroll this content.

description: Tooltip content must be reachable by all users, including screen reader and keyboard users.
recommendedFix:
Making tooltips accessible can be accomplished in two distinct ways:

- Make your tooltips accessible by using **manually**-activated tooltips. Please see [this section](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/524#heading-for-manuallyactivated-tooltips) in the Tooltips Knowledge Base article.
- Make your tooltips accessible by using **automatically**-activated tooltips. Please see [this section](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/524#heading-for-automaticallyactivated-tooltips) in the Tooltips Knowledge Base article.
  - **Note:** If you elect to use automatically-activated tooltips, these tooltips must convert to manually-activated tooltips when they are displayed on smaller viewports with a responsive layout. Please see the section regarding [Tooltip that is only available on smaller viewports](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/524#heading-tooltip-that-is-only-available-on-smaller-viewports) for more information on mobile responsive tooltips and a code sample illustrating this functionality.

Once you have decided which type of tooltip to implement (manual or automatic), please make a comment on this issue to let us know, and then include this issue in an upcoming QA or reach out to your CSM to have this content audited. description: Navigation menus that open on hover must be able to be triggered by keyboard and screen reader users.
recommendedFix:
Depending on the desired functionality of the menu, there are two approaches that can be taken for the top-level elements:

* If the top-level navigation item only actuates a menu and **does not** navigate to a new page when activated, mark it up as a button (`<button>`). See [this code sample](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/529#heading-menubar-where-menu-triggers-are-buttons) for guidance.
* If the top-level navigation item must link to a new page **and** actuate a menu, add an adjacent button that actuates the menu. See [this code sample](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/529#heading-menubar-where-menu-triggers-use-both-a-link-and-a-button) for guidance.
* If styling constraints do not allow for a visible button, this button could be visually hidden by default and become visible only when receiving focus, as shown in this [code sample](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/529#heading-menubar-where-menu-triggers-use-a-link-and-a-button-that-becomes-visible-on-focus).

description: Keyboard and screen reader users do not have their focus moved to this modal dialog when it opens.
recommendedFix:
Set the keyboard focus to the [most appropriate element](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/820#heading-moving-focus-into-a-modal-dialog-when-it-opens) inside this modal dialog, depending on the content it contains. All of the following solutions are acceptable, and you are free to decide which solution feels the most "appropriate" to you in this use case.

1. To the close (X) button, if one is used.
1. To the visible heading that labels the modal dialog, if one is used.
1. To the modal dialog wrapper itself (the element with both `role="dialog"` and `aria-modal="true"`).
1. To the primary call to action (CTA) element (such as an "OK" button), or the element for the least destructive action in a set of CTAs (like "Cancel" next to a button for "Delete").

**Note:** in order to set focus on an element that cannot natively receive focus (like a heading or the wrapper element), add the attribute `tabindex="-1"` to it.

description: Keyboard users are able to focus on elements outside of this modal dialog while it is open.

- An `<h2>` should head each major section of the page.

description: Errors are not identified to screen reader users.
recommendedFix:
Ensure that screen reader users are informed of the errors present for these form fields.

There are a number of ways that this can be addressed. Ideally, add an `aria-describedby` attribute and set focus on the first form field with an error. The `aria-describedby` attribute should be placed on the affected form field. It takes the `ID` of the element that contains the description of the error. If the form field is described by more than one element, you can set the `aria-describedby` attribute to a space-separated list of IDs.

Some alternative approaches are the following:

* Add an `aria-invalid` attribute to the `<input>` elements with errors. Ideally this is accompanied by setting focus on the first `<input>` with an error.
* Utilize the browser error alerts to indicate this information.

description: Focus indicators for actionable elements must be present and meet contrast requirements.
recommendedFix:
A focus indicator must always be visible and have at least 3:1 contrast.

It is best to intentionally style the focus indicator for all links, buttons, fields, etc. We encourage you to change the shape somehow (add a border, box, underline, etc.) as well as choose a color that has sufficient contrast with either the background of the page (if placed outside of the element) or the element itself (if placed inside of the element).

description: This live filter region requires additional ARIA markup to assist screen reader users in understanding what this section is for, and where it begins and ends.
recommendedFix:
Wrap both the text field and the content that it filters in a `<section>` tag or a `<div>` with `role=“region”` so that screen reader users can tell that they are related. 

Give this wrapper element a generic `aria-label` attribute value that broadly identifies what kind of content is being filtered. For example, “location filter” or “product filter”. 

See the [wrapper markup section](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/922#heading-wrapper) of the Knowledge Base article on Live Filters.

description: Screen Reader only text must be provided to describe the relationship between the live filter and its content.
recommendedFix:
Add screen reader only text inside of the filter region and before the input that provides instructions on how to use this live filter. 

For example, "The following text field filters the results that follow as you type."  Extend this screen reader only statement with additional instruction text tailored to your content and functionality.

description: Content changes are not announced as users enter text in the live filter input.
recommendedFix: Use a “live region” to announce when the filtered content changes as the user types in the text field. To accomplish this, add a visually hidden container, and give this container the `aria-live=”assertive”` attribute. When results are found, insert text into this container similar to "[#] results available". When no results are found, insert text like "no results available" so that users know that they should probably stop typing and try a different search term.

description: Images that lack alt attributes make it impossible for screen reader users to know what the image depicts.
recommendedFix:
Ensure each image has an `alt` attribute. The content of the alt attribute depends on the image type.

If an image is **informative** (i.e. provides information not conveyed in other ways), add an `alt` attribute to the image which conveys the information provided by it.
If an image is **decorative** (i.e. does not contribute any meaningful information), give the image an empty `alt` attribute (`alt=“”`).

description: Text that functions as a heading should be marked up as such.
recommendedFix:
Mark this text up as a heading.

Headings provide structure for screen reader users. When marking text up as a heading, verify that the page maintains a logical outline structure. For example; 

- Each page needs a single `<h1>` heading that describes the main purpose of the page.

description: Images that lack alt attributes make it impossible for screen reader users to know what the image depicts.
recommendedFix:
Ensure each image has an `alt` attribute. The content of the alt attribute depends on the image type.

If an image is **informative** (i.e. provides information not conveyed in other ways), add an `alt` attribute to the image which conveys the information provided by it.
If an image is **decorative** (i.e. does not contribute any meaningful information), give the image an empty `alt` attribute (`alt=“”`).

For more advice on determining which images are decorative or informative, visit our Knowledge Base Article: [The Art of Alt Attributes](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/472).

description: This autocomplete lacks instructions for screen reader users.
recommendedFix:
Add clear, succinct instructions as screen-reader-only text, then associate them with the input field using the `aria-describedby` attribute. See the [section about instructions](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/427#heading-instructions-for-screen-reader-users) in the Autocompletes Knowledge Base article for more information.

For the best user experience possible, conditionally add `aria-hidden="true"` to this text element when the input field is not focused so that screen reader users won't encounter it as they navigate the page.

affectedItem: "Date and Time:" fields > time autocomplete results
description: These autocomplete results are missing critical ARIA attributes.
recommendedFix:
Add `role="listbox"` to the `<ul>` containing the results. Add an `aria-labelledby` attribute to the `<ul>`. The `aria-labelledby` attribute takes the ID of the `<label>` associated with the autocomplete's text input field.

Next, add `role="option"` to each `<li>`. Ensure that each of these list items has a unique `id` attribute value.

See [this section](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/427#heading-simple-listbox-popup) of the Autocompletes Knowledge Base article for additional guidance.

description: This field is not marked up as an inline autocomplete
recommendedFix:
If a popup listbox is not also used, add `aria-autocomplete="inline"` to the input text field.

If a popup listbox is used in addition to the inline autocomplete, add `aria-autocomplete="both"` to the input text field. 

See [this section of the Autocompletes KB article](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/427#heading-inline-suggestions) for more guidance.

affectedItem: "Date and Time:" fields > time autocomplete field
description: This text input with autocomplete functionality is missing critical ARIA attributes.
recommendedFix:
Add an `aria-autocomplete` attribute. Set the value of the attribute to `list` if displaying a list of options; set the value to `inline` if displaying a single autocomplete option within the input field; or set the value to `both` if using a combination.

Additionally, if a list popup is used:

1. Add `aria-controls="[ID of list element]"`.
1. Add `aria-haspopup="listbox"`.
1. Add `aria-expanded` and set its value to `true` or `false` based on the visibility of the list. Update this value as necessary as the user interacts with the autocomplete.

See [this section of the Autocompletes KB article](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/427#heading-text-input) for complete guidance on marking up this text input as an autocomplete.

affectedItem: "Date and Time:" fields > time autocomplete results
description: The number of autocomplete results available is not announced to screen reader users.
recommendedFix:
Ensure that the current number of available results is read out to screen reader users. Follow [the guidance in this section of the Autocompletes KB article](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/427#heading-results-found-announcements-for-screen-reader-users) for how to make this information available for screen reader users. 

Additionally, refer to the [Listbox Popup code sample](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/427#heading-listbox-popup).

description: The modal dialog container is not labeled.
recommendedFix:
Provide a [label using one of the following methods](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/820#heading-labelling). All of these solutions are acceptable, but some may be easier to implement than others depending on the content within the modal dialog.

1. Add a heading (preferably an `<h1>`, but `<h2>` is acceptable), then associate it with the modal dialog wrapper by giving that heading a unique `id` and referencing it with an `aria-labelledby` attribute on the wrapper element (the element with `role="dialog"` and `aria-modal="true"`).
  * If a heading describing the contents of the modal dialog already exists, you can use that heading instead.
  * This heading is most helpful when it is visible for all users, but for strict WCAG conformance it can be made visible only to screen reader users instead.
1. Alternatively, add an `aria-label` attribute to the wrapper element (the element with `role="dialog"` and `aria-modal="true"`) describing the purpose of the modal dialog.

description: Errors are not identified to screen reader users.
recommendedFix:
Ensure that screen reader users are informed of the errors present for these form fields.

There are a number of ways that this can be addressed. Ideally, add an `aria-describedby` attribute and set focus on the first form field with an error. The `aria-describedby` attribute should be placed on the affected form field. It takes the `ID` of the element that contains the description of the error. If the form field is described by more than one element, you can set the `aria-describedby` attribute to a space-separated list of IDs.

Some alternative approaches are the following:

* Add an `aria-invalid` attribute to the `<input>` elements with errors. Ideally this is accompanied by setting focus on the first `<input>` with an error.
* Utilize the browser error alerts to indicate this information.

description: Elements that function as links must be marked up as such so that screen reader users will identify them as actionable and they will be usable by keyboard users.
recommendedFix:
Preferably, links should be marked up as semantic HTML `<a>` elements.

Less preferably, ensure that custom link elements include `role=“link”` and `tabindex=“0”`, and have the appropriate scripting in place so that the element can be selected by keyboard users using the `Enter` key and by mouse click.

description: The information contained in charts or graphs may not be accessible for all users.
recommendedFix:
Charts or graphs that rely on visual appearance (such as color alone) to convey meaning, may not convey that information to color blind and screen reader users. 

**For color blind users:**
Ensure that information is not conveyed by color alone, and has a second visual indicator, such as shape, outlining, etc. (See the [Charts and graphs section](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/863#heading-charts-and-graphs) of this article for more information.)

**For screen reader users:**
Add a table for screen reader users which communicates the same information provided by the graph. You might also consider making the table visible to everyone, and not just to screen reader users, as other users may benefit from having this information presented in another way.

description: Content that functions as a list should be indicated as such to screen reader users.
recommendedFix:
When a series of similar items is grouped together in a meaningful or deliberate way, this should be conveyed to screen reader users.

Use standard HTML to mark up all such content as a list. Ensure that the list items are the direct children of the wrapping `<ol>`, `<ul>`, or `<dl>` tag.

description: When content is marked up as a table, but is not semantically a table, it can be confusing for screen reader users.
recommendedFix:
Preferably remove the `<table>` wrapping this content.

Less preferably, add the attribute `role="presentation"` to the `<table>` tag. Ensure that the content is responsive so that it does not require horizontal scrolling.

description: Text within images causes problems for screen reader users and users of magnification technology.
recommendedFix:
**Preferred Remediation:**

- Extract the text from the image and place it on the page using HTML; use CSS to style and position it as desired superimposed over the image(s).
_Or…_
- Place the text on the page adjacent to the image, similar to a caption.

**Alternative Remediation:**

We recognize solving this issue using the preferred method may not be feasible for all situations, so completing all of the numbered steps is an alternative solution to close this issue: 

1. Add all of the text from the image, and [any other visual information necessary for understanding](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/472), to an `alt` attribute on the image. If the `alt` attribute is already present, ensure it accurately reflects the text within the image and that the other steps for this recommendation are followed.
1. Ensure that the image is reasonably readable up to 200% zoom.
1. (Optional) Add only the text from the image as a title attribute to the image to assist magnification users.

**Reminder:** When overlaying text on an image, make sure the [text has proper contrast](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/862#heading-text-over-images-and-complex-backgrounds) to the background image. 

Please note, this method will not meet WCAG 1.4.5, but it has been determined to be an acceptable exception to resolve this issue. **By choosing the “Alternative Remediation” method described above you are accepting any accessibility liability risk for this content and understand that this remediation option does not comply with the associated WCAG guidelines which will continue to present some accessibility issues.**

After this alternative remediation has been successfully implemented, we will downgrade this issue to a warning (P3) with a comment indicating as such and set the issue status to Not Fixing. This status will not prevent you from obtaining a Letter of Conformance and it is encouraged that you attempt to fully remediate this content using the preferred remediation methods during future updates.

description: Keyboard and screen reader users do not have their focus moved to this modal dialog when it opens.
recommendedFix:
Set the keyboard focus to the [most appropriate element](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/820#heading-moving-focus-into-a-modal-dialog-when-it-opens) inside this modal dialog, depending on the content it contains. All of the following solutions are acceptable, and you are free to decide which solution feels the most "appropriate" to you in this use case.

1. To the close (X) button, if one is used.
1. To the visible heading that labels the modal dialog, if one is used.
1. To the modal dialog wrapper itself (the element with both `role="dialog"` and `aria-modal="true"`).
1. To the primary call to action (CTA) element (such as an "OK" button), or the element for the least destructive action in a set of CTAs (like "Cancel" next to a button for "Delete").

**Note:** in order to set focus on an element that cannot natively receive focus (like a heading or the wrapper element), add the attribute `tabindex="-1"` to it.

pageName: Reports Main Page+ Report History Mini Modal
description: The modal dialog container is not labeled.
recommendedFix:
Provide a [label using one of the following methods](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/820#heading-labelling). All of these solutions are acceptable, but some may be easier to implement than others depending on the content within the modal dialog.

1. Add a heading (preferably an `<h1>`, but `<h2>` is acceptable), then associate it with the modal dialog wrapper by giving that heading a unique `id` and referencing it with an `aria-labelledby` attribute on the wrapper element (the element with `role="dialog"` and `aria-modal="true"`).
  * If a heading describing the contents of the modal dialog already exists, you can use that heading instead.
  * This heading is most helpful when it is visible for all users, but for strict WCAG conformance it can be made visible only to screen reader users instead.
1. Alternatively, add an `aria-label` attribute to the wrapper element (the element with `role="dialog"` and `aria-modal="true"`) describing the purpose of the modal dialog.

pageName: Reports Main Page+ Report History Mini Modal
description: Keyboard users are able to focus on elements outside of this modal dialog while it is open.
recommendedFix: Do not allow Tab or Shift + Tab to move focus outside of a modal dialog. See the [code sample provided in the related Knowledge Base article](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/820#heading-trapping-keyboard-focus) for additional details.

If this element is no longer available on the page, then focus should be moved to another element as close as possible to where that element was.

If this modal dialog was opened automatically when the page loaded, then move focus on to the `<body>` element.

Do not [add these attributes](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/820#heading--do-not-dynamically-add-these-attributes-while-a-users-focus-is-inside) dynamically after the user's focus has been moved to it or into it.

description: This modal dialog contains one or more heading levels in an illogical order.
recommendedFix:
Verify that the modal dialog maintains a logical outline structure. For example, 

- Each modal dialog can begin with a single `<h1>` heading that describes the main purpose of the modal dialog. If this is not possible, a less preferable option would be to begin this modal dialog with an `<h2>`.

description: Text within images causes problems for screen reader users and users of magnification technology.
recommendedFix:

**Reminder:** When overlaying text on an image, make sure the [text has proper contrast](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/862#heading-text-over-images-and-complex-backgrounds) to the background image.

description: Errors are not identified to screen reader users.
recommendedFix:
Ensure that screen reader users are informed of the errors present for these form fields.

There are a number of ways that this can be addressed. Ideally, add an `aria-describedby` attribute and set focus on the first form field with an error. The `aria-describedby` attribute should be placed on the affected form field. It takes the `ID` of the element that contains the description of the error. If the form field is described by more than one element, you can set the `aria-describedby` attribute to a space-separated list of IDs.

Some alternative approaches are the following:

* Add an `aria-invalid` attribute to the `<input>` elements with errors. Ideally this is accompanied by setting focus on the first `<input>` with an error.
* Utilize the browser error alerts to indicate this information.

description: The modal dialog container is not labeled.
recommendedFix:
Provide a [label using one of the following methods](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/820#heading-labelling). All of these solutions are acceptable, but some may be easier to implement than others depending on the content within the modal dialog.

1. Add a heading (preferably an `<h1>`, but `<h2>` is acceptable), then associate it with the modal dialog wrapper by giving that heading a unique `id` and referencing it with an `aria-labelledby` attribute on the wrapper element (the element with `role="dialog"` and `aria-modal="true"`).
  * If a heading describing the contents of the modal dialog already exists, you can use that heading instead.
  * This heading is most helpful when it is visible for all users, but for strict WCAG conformance it can be made visible only to screen reader users instead.
1. Alternatively, add an `aria-label` attribute to the wrapper element (the element with `role="dialog"` and `aria-modal="true"`) describing the purpose of the modal dialog.

description: Keyboard and screen reader users do not have their focus moved to this modal dialog when it opens.
recommendedFix:
Set the keyboard focus to the [most appropriate element](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/820#heading-moving-focus-into-a-modal-dialog-when-it-opens) inside this modal dialog, depending on the content it contains. All of the following solutions are acceptable, and you are free to decide which solution feels the most "appropriate" to you in this use case.

1. To the close (X) button, if one is used.
1. To the visible heading that labels the modal dialog, if one is used.
1. To the modal dialog wrapper itself (the element with both `role="dialog"` and `aria-modal="true"`).
1. To the primary call to action (CTA) element (such as an "OK" button), or the element for the least destructive action in a set of CTAs (like "Cancel" next to a button for "Delete").

**Note:** in order to set focus on an element that cannot natively receive focus (like a heading or the wrapper element), add the attribute `tabindex="-1"` to it.

description: Tooltip content must be reachable by all users, including screen reader and keyboard users.
recommendedFix:
Making tooltips accessible can be accomplished in two distinct ways:

- Make your tooltips accessible by using **manually**-activated tooltips. Please see [this section](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/524#heading-for-manuallyactivated-tooltips) in the Tooltips Knowledge Base article.
- Make your tooltips accessible by using **automatically**-activated tooltips. Please see [this section](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/524#heading-for-automaticallyactivated-tooltips) in the Tooltips Knowledge Base article.
  - **Note:** If you elect to use automatically-activated tooltips, these tooltips must convert to manually-activated tooltips when they are displayed on smaller viewports with a responsive layout. Please see the section regarding [Tooltip that is only available on smaller viewports](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/524#heading-tooltip-that-is-only-available-on-smaller-viewports) for more information on mobile responsive tooltips and a code sample illustrating this functionality.

Once you have decided which type of tooltip to implement (manual or automatic), please make a comment on this issue to let us know, and then include this issue in an upcoming QA or reach out to your CSM to have this content audited. We will then set this issue to Not Applicable and add new issues as needed to address the content.

description: Errors are not identified to screen reader users.
recommendedFix:
Ensure that screen reader users are informed of the errors present for these form fields.

There are a number of ways that this can be addressed. Ideally, add an `aria-describedby` attribute and set focus on the first form field with an error. The `aria-describedby` attribute should be placed on the affected form field. It takes the `ID` of the element that contains the description of the error. If the form field is described by more than one element, you can set the `aria-describedby` attribute to a space-separated list of IDs.

Some alternative approaches are the following:

* Add an `aria-invalid` attribute to the `<input>` elements with errors. Ideally this is accompanied by setting focus on the first `<input>` with an error.

description: The modal dialog container is not labeled.
recommendedFix:
Provide a [label using one of the following methods](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/820#heading-labelling). All of these solutions are acceptable, but some may be easier to implement than others depending on the content within the modal dialog.

1. Add a heading (preferably an `<h1>`, but `<h2>` is acceptable), then associate it with the modal dialog wrapper by giving that heading a unique `id` and referencing it with an `aria-labelledby` attribute on the wrapper element (the element with `role="dialog"` and `aria-modal="true"`).

1. Alternatively, add an `aria-label` attribute to the wrapper element (the element with `role="dialog"` and `aria-modal="true"`) describing the purpose of the modal dialog.

description: Elements with positive tabindex values cause problems for keyboard and screen reader users.

description: Text within images causes problems for screen reader users and users of magnification technology.
recommendedFix:
**Preferred Remediation:**

- Extract the text from the image and place it on the page using HTML; use CSS to style and position it as desired superimposed over the image(s).
_Or…_
- Place the text on the page adjacent to the image, similar to a caption.

**Alternative Remediation:**

We recognize solving this issue using the preferred method may not be feasible for all situations, so completing all of the numbered steps is an alternative solution to close this issue: 

1. Add all of the text from the image, and [any other visual information necessary for understanding](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/472), to an `alt` attribute on the image. If the `alt` attribute is already present, ensure it accurately reflects the text within the image and that the other steps for this recommendation are followed.
1. Ensure that the image is reasonably readable up to 200% zoom.
1. (Optional) Add only the text from the image as a title attribute to the image to assist magnification users.

**Reminder:** When overlaying text on an image, make sure the [text has proper contrast](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/862#heading-text-over-images-and-complex-backgrounds) to the background image. 

Please note, this method will not meet WCAG 1.4.5, but it has been determined to be an acceptable exception to resolve this issue. **By choosing the “Alternative Remediation” method described above you are accepting any accessibility liability risk for this content and understand that this remediation option does not comply with the associated WCAG guidelines which will continue to present some accessibility issues.**

After this alternative remediation has been successfully implemented, we will downgrade this issue to a warning (P3) with a comment indicating as such and set the issue status to Not Fixing. This status will not prevent you from obtaining a Letter of Conformance and it is encouraged that you attempt to fully remediate this content using the preferred remediation methods during future updates.

description: This content is marked up as a table; however it is semantically a list.
recommendedFix: Remove the `<table>` wrapping this content and mark this up as a standard HTML list as appropriate to the content.

description: This page lacks an <h1> heading.
recommendedFix:
Add an `<h1>` heading to this page at the start of the main content that describes its topic or purpose. Common examples include "About Us", "Contact Us", "Terms of Use", etc.

If this does not conform to styling, instead add this text as screen reader only text, and then wrap that text in an `<h1>` tag.

description: When an asterisk is used as a symbol, but the meaning of the symbol is not defined, it can cause confusion for some users.
recommendedFix: Define the meaning of the asterisks at the start of the form. For example, add text that says: "* indicates a required field" or similar.

description: All form fields must be properly labeled.
recommendedFix: Ensure all form fields have a visible label (typically via a `<label>` tag) which is properly associated with its field (via the `for` attribute, which takes the value of the `id` from the form field).

description: Form fields that are required must be programmatically indicated to screen reader users.
recommendedFix: Preferably, the `required` attribute should be used or less preferred, use an `aria-required` attribute.

description: Alert messages must be conveyed to screen reader users.
recommendedFix: Place a `role="alert"` on the element that wraps each message. Ensure that this role is always on the element from the moment it is created until it is destroyed. This role will not work if it is added to an already existing DOM element.

description: Errors are not identified to screen reader users.
recommendedFix:
Ensure that screen reader users are informed of the errors present for these form fields.

There are a number of ways that this can be addressed. Ideally, add an `aria-describedby` attribute and set focus on the first form field with an error. The `aria-describedby` attribute should be placed on the affected form field. It takes the `ID` of the element that contains the description of the error. If the form field is described by more than one element, you can set the `aria-describedby` attribute to a space-separated list of IDs.

Some alternative approaches are the following:

* Add an `aria-invalid` attribute to the `<input>` elements with errors. Ideally this is accompanied by setting focus on the first `<input>` with an error.
* Utilize the browser error alerts to indicate this information.

affectedItem: "x" and checkmark icons on error/approved messages
description: There is an aria-hidden="true" attribute wrapping this content, which causes this content to be invisible to screen reader users.
recommendedFix: Remove the `aria-hidden="true"` attribute from this content.

description: SVG elements depicting important information need to be properly labeled.
recommendedFix:
Add `role="img"` and `aria-labelledby` attributes to each `<svg>` tag, then add a `<title>` tag within the `<svg>` tag and give this `<title>` tag a unique `id` attribute. Ensure the `<title>` is a direct descendant of the `<svg>` tag and that the `<svg>` tag’s `aria-labelledby` attribute holds the `<title>` tag’s `id` value.
			
Alternatively, give the `<svg>` tag `role=”img”` and `aria-label` attributes. Ensure the `aria-label` accurately and concisely describes the content of each image.

description: Instructions that are not programmatically associated with their relevant form fields may not be available to screen reader users.
recommendedFix: Associate the instructions with their relevant form fields via the `aria-describedby` attribute. The `aria-describedby` attribute should be placed on the relevant form field, and should be assigned the `id` of the instructions to be associated. If the field is described by more than one element, you can set the `aria-describedby` attribute to a space separated list of `id` values.

description: Text that functions as a heading should be marked up as such.
recommendedFix:
Mark this text up as a heading.

Headings provide structure for screen reader users. When marking text up as a heading, verify that the page maintains a logical outline structure. For example; 

- Each page needs a single `<h1>` heading that describes the main purpose of the page.
- An `<h2>` should head each major section of the page.
- Subsequent heading levels (`<h3>` through `<h6>`) should be related to a parent `<h2>` and should not skip heading levels.

description: Content that functions as a list should be indicated as such to screen reader users.
recommendedFix:
When a series of similar items is grouped together in a meaningful or deliberate way, this should be conveyed to screen reader users.

Use standard HTML to mark up all such content as a list. Ensure that the list items are the direct children of the wrapping `<ol>`, `<ul>`, or `<dl>` tag.

description: This live filter region requires additional ARIA markup to assist screen reader users in understanding what this section is for, and where it begins and ends.
recommendedFix:
Wrap both the text field and the content that it filters in a `<section>` tag or a `<div>` with `role=“region”` so that screen reader users can tell that they are related. 

Give this wrapper element a generic `aria-label` attribute value that broadly identifies what kind of content is being filtered. For example, “location filter” or “product filter”. 

See the [wrapper markup section](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/922#heading-wrapper) of the Knowledge Base article on Live Filters.

description: Screen Reader only text must be provided to describe the relationship between the live filter and its content.
recommendedFix:
Add screen reader only text inside of the filter region and before the input that provides instructions on how to use this live filter. 

For example, "The following text field filters the results that follow as you type."  Extend this screen reader only statement with additional instruction text tailored to your content and functionality.

description: Content changes are not announced as users enter text in the live filter input.
recommendedFix: Use a “live region” to announce when the filtered content changes as the user types in the text field. To accomplish this, add a visually hidden container, and give this container the `aria-live=”assertive”` attribute. When results are found, insert text into this container similar to "[#] results available". When no results are found, insert text like "no results available" so that users know that they should probably stop typing and try a different search term.

description: Visually disabled buttons must be programmatically indicated to screen reader users, and should not receive keyboard focus.
