description: These tab controls are missing critical ARIA attributes.
recommendedFix:
* Add `role="tab"` to the triggering elements. 
* Add an `aria-controls` attribute to each element with the `role="tab"`. Ensure that the value of the `aria-controls` attribute is the `id` of the tabpanel it is intended to control.
* Add an `aria-selected` attribute to each of these elements as well. Set its value to "true" on the tab element that is currently active, and "false" for all other tabs. Ensure the value of this attribute is dynamically updated as the user interacts with the tabs to indicate the active tab at all times.

description: These tab panels are missing critical ARIA attributes.
recommendedFix:
* Add `role="tabpanel"` to the container element wrapping the content controlled by the related element with `role=”tab”`.
* Add the attribute `aria-labelledby` to the element with `role=”tabpanel”` and set its value equal to the `id` of the tab element that controls it.
* Optionally, as a usability best practice, add `tabindex="0"` to each tab panel to make the component easier for inexperienced keyboard-only users to navigate.

description: Keyboard users are unable to interact with these tabs as expected.
recommendedFix:
Keyboard and screen reader users will expect to be able to interact with these tabs in the following ways:

1. Only the currently selected tab should be focusable via the tab key. To do this, add a `tabindex="-1"` to all non-selected tabs.
1. Ensure that the `Left` and `Right` arrow keys allow the user to traverse the options in the tablist.
1. Tabs can be activated automatically or manually. If they are activated automatically, the tabs will be selected as they are traversed via the arrow keys. If they are activated manually, they will be selected by pressing either the `Enter` or `Space` key. Ensure that the `aria-selected` and `tabindex` attributes are updated as the new tab is activated. See this [section about automatic versus manual activation](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/606#heading-automatic-versus-manual-tab-activation) in the related Knowledge Base article to learn more.

If these tabs are arranged vertically, ensure that users can use the `Up` and `Down` arrow keys (in addition to `Left` and `Right`) to traverse the tabs.

Optionally, you may additionally choose to allow users to use the `Home` and `End` keys to navigate to the start and end of the tablist.

description: Drag and drop features must be accessible to keyboard users and screen reader users.
recommendedFix: Provide controls for keyboard users that will enable movement of the element. For example, allow keyboard users to move the window using the Left, Right, Up, and Down arrow keys. Ensure these controls are properly labeled for screen reader users.

description: Additional content is only revealed on hover, which is inaccessible to screen reader and keyboard users.
recommendedFix:
Make all content reachable and visible to screen reader and keyboard users. There are multiple ways to do this, depending on the specific use case. Start by reading through the standard techniques below:

- For **tooltips**, read about [handling content that is shown automatically on hover](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/524#heading-for-automaticallyactivated-tooltips).

description: When content is marked up as a table, but is not semantically a table, it can be confusing for screen reader users.
recommendedFix:
Preferably remove the `<table>` wrapping this content.

Less preferably, add the attribute `role="presentation"` to the `<table>` tag. Ensure that the content is responsive so that it does not require horizontal scrolling.

description: The information contained in charts or graphs may not be accessible for all users.
recommendedFix:
Charts or graphs that rely on visual appearance (such as color alone) to convey meaning, may not convey that information to color blind and screen reader users. 

**For color blind users:**
Ensure that information is not conveyed by color alone, and has a second visual indicator, such as shape, outlining, etc. (See the [Charts and graphs section](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/863#heading-charts-and-graphs) of this article for more information.)

**For screen reader users:**
Add a table for screen reader users which communicates the same information provided by the graph. You might also consider making the table visible to everyone, and not just to screen reader users, as other users may benefit from having this information presented in another way.

description: Buttons must have sufficient labels for all users.
recommendedFix: Add screen reader only text or an `aria-label` attribute to each button which tells users where it goes and/or what it does. Please note that the `title` attribute is not sufficient for button labeling.

description: Elements that control expandable content must be indicated to screen reader users.
recommendedFix: Add an `aria-controls` attribute to each element that controls expandable content and set the value of that attribute to equal the `id` of the tag that wraps the expanded content. Also add an `aria-expanded="true"` attribute to that same control element when content is expanded, and `aria-expanded="false"` otherwise.

description: Elements that function as buttons must be marked up as such so that screen reader users will identify them as actionable and they will be usable by keyboard users.
recommendedFix:
Preferably, buttons should be marked up as semantic HTML `<button>` elements.

Less preferably, ensure that custom button elements include `role="button”` and `tabindex=“0”`, and have the appropriate scripting in place so that the element can be selected by keyboard users using the `Enter` key and `Space` key, and by mouse click.

description: Tables with visible column and/or row headers must be properly indicated to screen readers.
recommendedFix:
Ensure that text serving as the header for each column is marked up in a `<th scope=“col”>`. 

Ensure that text serving as the header for each row (if present) is wrapped in a `<th scope=“row”>`. Often this text is the first cell in each row, [but not always](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/29#heading-not-always-the-first-row-or-first-column).

description: Images that lack alt attributes make it impossible for screen reader users to know what the image depicts.
recommendedFix:
Ensure each image has an `alt` attribute. The content of the alt attribute depends on the image type.

If an image is **informative** (i.e. provides information not conveyed in other ways), add an `alt` attribute to the image which conveys the information provided by it.
If an image is **decorative** (i.e. does not contribute any meaningful information), give the image an empty `alt` attribute (`alt=“”`).

For more advice on determining which images are decorative or informative, visit our Knowledge Base Article: [The Art of Alt Attributes](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/472).

description: Some regions require additional ARIA markup to assist screen reader users in understanding what a section is for, and where it begins and ends.
recommendedFix: Add a `role="region"` and an `aria-label` attribute that succinctly describes the purpose of each region to the element wrapping this content.

description: Text that functions as a heading should be marked up as such.
recommendedFix:
Mark this text up as a heading.

Headings provide structure for screen reader users. When marking text up as a heading, verify that the page maintains a logical outline structure. For example; 

- Each page needs a single `<h1>` heading that describes the main purpose of the page.
- An `<h2>` should head each major section of the page.
- Subsequent heading levels (`<h3>` through `<h6>`) should be related to a parent `<h2>` and should not skip heading levels.

description: All form fields must be properly labeled.

description: Custom select dropdowns can pose accessibility issues for keyboard and/or screen reader users.
recommendedFix:

description: When non-essential icons are not properly hidden from screen reader users, they can be announced as unrecognized characters.
recommendedFix:
Hide non-essential icons by moving them into their own `<span>`, or other inline tag, then giving the `<span>` an `aria-hidden="true"` attribute.

If a non-essential icon is already independently wrapped by an element, instead give this element an `aria-hidden="true"` attribute. Ensure that no other content is contained within the element wrapping the icon, as doing so may inadvertently or improperly hide the additional content from screen reader users.

description: Errors are not identified to screen reader users.
recommendedFix:
Ensure that screen reader users are informed of the errors present for these form fields.

There are a number of ways that this can be addressed. Ideally, add an `aria-describedby` attribute and set focus on the first form field with an error. The `aria-describedby` attribute should be placed on the affected form field. It takes the `ID` of the element that contains the description of the error. If the form field is described by more than one element, you can set the `aria-describedby` attribute to a space-separated list of IDs.

Some alternative approaches are the following:

* Add an `aria-invalid` attribute to the `<input>` elements with errors. Ideally this is accompanied by setting focus on the first `<input>` with an error.
* Utilize the browser error alerts to indicate this information.

description: Form field groupings must have a fieldset and legend.

The visual presentation of all instances of text & images of text presented in this color combination — across the entire site — should be modified to have a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1. Larger text with a size of at least 18pt (24px or 1.5em), or 14pt (18.66px or 1.2em) and bold (font-weight: 700 or more), only requires a minimum contrast ratio of 3:1.

**Note:** the color combination specified in this issue’s example may also be present elsewhere on your site. We recommend careful review and monitoring of all site colors to ensure ongoing, site wide compliance with color contrast requirements.

description: Unnecessary ARIA attributes can cause unexpected behavior for screen reader users.
recommendedFix: The presence of an unnecessary ARIA attribute can create unexpected behavior across various configurations. Remove the `aria-haspopup`, `aria-owns` attributes from the element.

description: Elements that control expandable content must be indicated to screen reader users.
recommendedFix: Add an `aria-controls` attribute to each element that controls expandable content and set the value of that attribute to equal the `id` of the tag that wraps the expanded content. Also add an `aria-expanded="true"` attribute to that same control element when content is expanded, and `aria-expanded="false"` otherwise.

description: Elements that function as buttons must be marked up as such so that screen reader users will identify them as actionable and they will be usable by keyboard users.

description: Focus indicators for actionable elements must be present and meet contrast requirements.
recommendedFix:
A focus indicator must always be visible and have at least 3:1 contrast.

It is best to intentionally style the focus indicator for all links, buttons, fields, etc. We encourage you to change the shape somehow (add a border, box, underline, etc.) as well as choose a color that has sufficient contrast with either the background of the page (if placed outside of the element) or the element itself (if placed inside of the element).

description: Toggle buttons need to convey their state to screen reader users.
recommendedFix: Add an `aria-pressed` attribute to this button. Ensure that the `aria-pressed` attribute correctly reflects the state of the button. The value of the attribute should be set to "true" when the button is pressed and "false" when it's not pressed.

description: Negative tabindex attributes on actionable elements removes them from the tab order.
recommendedFix: Remove the `tabindex` attribute from each element so that they can be focused by the keyboard when navigating with the `Tab` and `Shift + Tab` keys.

description: The modal dialog container is not labeled.
recommendedFix:
Provide a [label using one of the following methods](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/820#heading-labelling). All of these solutions are acceptable, but some may be easier to implement than others depending on the content within the modal dialog.

1. Add a heading (preferably an `<h1>`, but `<h2>` is acceptable), then associate it with the modal dialog wrapper by giving that heading a unique `id` and referencing it with an `aria-labelledby` attribute on the wrapper element (the element with `role="dialog"` and `aria-modal="true"`).
  * If a heading describing the contents of the modal dialog already exists, you can use that heading instead.
  * This heading is most helpful when it is visible for all users, but for strict WCAG conformance it can be made visible only to screen reader users instead.
1. Alternatively, add an `aria-label` attribute to the wrapper element (the element with `role="dialog"` and `aria-modal="true"`) describing the purpose of the modal dialog.

description: Closing this modal dialog does not return the user to the element that opened it.
recommendedFix:
When this modal dialog closes, return focus to the element that triggered this modal dialog to open.

If this element is no longer available on the page, then focus should be moved to another element as close as possible to where that element was.

If this modal dialog was opened automatically when the page loaded, then move focus on to the `<body>` element.

description: This modal dialog is missing necessary ARIA attributes.
recommendedFix: Ensure the attributes `role="dialog"` and `aria-modal="true"` are present on the wrapper element of this modal dialog. Do not [add these attributes](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/820#heading--do-not-dynamically-add-these-attributes-while-a-users-focus-is-inside) dynamically after the user's focus has been moved to it or into it.

description: Text that functions as a heading should be marked up as such.
recommendedFix:
Mark this text up as a heading.

Headings provide structure for screen reader users. When marking text up as a heading, verify that the page maintains a logical outline structure. For example; 

- Each page needs a single `<h1>` heading that describes the main purpose of the page.
- An `<h2>` should head each major section of the page.
- Subsequent heading levels (`<h3>` through `<h6>`) should be related to a parent `<h2>` and should not skip heading levels.

description: Unactionable elements should not have tabindex=”0”.

description: Focus indicators for actionable elements must be present and meet contrast requirements.

A focus indicator must always be visible and have at least 3:1 contrast.

It is best to intentionally style the focus indicator for all links, buttons, fields, etc. We encourage you to change the shape somehow (add a border, box, underline, etc.) as well as choose a color that has sufficient contrast with either the background of the page (if placed outside of the element) or the element itself (if placed inside of the element).

description: Images that lack alt attributes make it impossible for screen reader users to know what the image depicts.
recommendedFix:
Ensure each image has an `alt` attribute. The content of the alt attribute depends on the image type.

If an image is **informative** (i.e. provides information not conveyed in other ways), add an `alt` attribute to the image which conveys the information provided by it.
If an image is **decorative** (i.e. does not contribute any meaningful information), give the image an empty `alt` attribute (`alt=“”`).

For more advice on determining which images are decorative or informative, visit our Knowledge Base Article: [The Art of Alt Attributes](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/472).

description: Tooltip content must be reachable by all users, including screen reader and keyboard users.
recommendedFix:
Making tooltips accessible can be accomplished in two distinct ways:

- Make your tooltips accessible by using **manually**-activated tooltips. Please see [this section](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/524#heading-for-manuallyactivated-tooltips) in the Tooltips Knowledge Base article.
- Make your tooltips accessible by using **automatically**-activated tooltips. Please see [this section](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/524#heading-for-automaticallyactivated-tooltips) in the Tooltips Knowledge Base article.
  - **Note:** If you elect to use automatically-activated tooltips, these tooltips must convert to manually-activated tooltips when they are displayed on smaller viewports with a responsive layout. Please see the section regarding [Tooltip that is only available on smaller viewports](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/524#heading-tooltip-that-is-only-available-on-smaller-viewports) for more information on mobile responsive tooltips and a code sample illustrating this functionality.

Once you have decided which type of tooltip to implement (manual or automatic), please make a comment on this issue to let us know, and then include this issue in an upcoming QA or reach out to your CSM to have this content audited. We will then set this issue to Not Applicable and add new issues as needed to address the content.

recommendedFix: Ensure all form fields have a visible label (typically via a `<label>` tag) which is properly associated with its field (via the `for` attribute, which takes the value of the `id` from the form field).

affectedItem: Tables wrapping action buttons and expanadable buttons
description: When content is marked up as a table, but is not semantically a table, it can be confusing for screen reader users.
recommendedFix:
Preferably remove the `<table>` wrapping this content.

Less preferably, add the attribute `role="presentation"` to the `<table>` tag. Ensure that the content is responsive so that it does not require horizontal scrolling.

affectedItem: "Commitment Invoice Details" to "Invoice Items" expandable buttons
description: Images that lack alt attributes make it impossible for screen reader users to know what the image depicts.
recommendedFix:
Ensure each image has an `alt` attribute. The content of the alt attribute depends on the image type.

If an image is **informative** (i.e. provides information not conveyed in other ways), add an `alt` attribute to the image which conveys the information provided by it.
If an image is **decorative** (i.e. does not contribute any meaningful information), give the image an empty `alt` attribute (`alt=“”`).

For more advice on determining which images are decorative or informative, visit our Knowledge Base Article: [The Art of Alt Attributes](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/472).

affectedItem: "Commitment Invoice Details" to "Invoice Items" expandable buttons
description: Elements that function as buttons must be marked up as such so that screen reader users will identify them as actionable and they will be usable by keyboard users.
recommendedFix:
Preferably, buttons should be marked up as semantic HTML `<button>` elements.

Less preferably, ensure that custom button elements include `role="button”` and `tabindex=“0”`, and have the appropriate scripting in place so that the element can be selected by keyboard users using the `Enter` key and `Space` key, and by mouse click.

affectedItem: "Commitment Invoice Details" to "Invoice Items" expandable buttons
description: Elements that control expandable content must be indicated to screen reader users.
recommendedFix: Add an `aria-controls` attribute to each element that controls expandable content and set the value of that attribute to equal the `id` of the tag that wraps the expanded content. Also add an `aria-expanded="true"` attribute to that same control element when content is expanded, and `aria-expanded="false"` otherwise.

description: Tooltip content must be reachable by all users, including screen reader and keyboard users.
recommendedFix:
Making tooltips accessible can be accomplished in two distinct ways:

- Make your tooltips accessible by using **manually**-activated tooltips. Please see [this section](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/524#heading-for-manuallyactivated-tooltips) in the Tooltips Knowledge Base article.
- Make your tooltips accessible by using **automatically**-activated tooltips. Please see [this section](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/524#heading-for-automaticallyactivated-tooltips) in the Tooltips Knowledge Base article.
  - **Note:** If you elect to use automatically-activated tooltips, these tooltips must convert to manually-activated tooltips when they are displayed on smaller viewports with a responsive layout. Please see the section regarding [Tooltip that is only available on smaller viewports](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/524#heading-tooltip-that-is-only-available-on-smaller-viewports) for more information on mobile responsive tooltips and a code sample illustrating this functionality.

Once you have decided which type of tooltip to implement (manual or automatic), please make a comment on this issue to let us know, and then include this issue in an upcoming QA or reach out to your CSM to have this content audited. We will then set this issue to Not Applicable and add new issues as needed to address the content.

description: Keyboard and screen reader users do not have their focus moved to this modal dialog when it opens.
recommendedFix:
Set the keyboard focus to the [most appropriate element](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/820#heading-moving-focus-into-a-modal-dialog-when-it-opens) inside this modal dialog, depending on the content it contains. All of the following solutions are acceptable, and you are free to decide which solution feels the most "appropriate" to you in this use case.

1. To the close (X) button, if one is used.
1. To the visible heading that labels the modal dialog, if one is used.
1. To the modal dialog wrapper itself (the element with both `role="dialog"` and `aria-modal="true"`).
1. To the primary call to action (CTA) element (such as an "OK" button), or the element for the least destructive action in a set of CTAs (like "Cancel" next to a button for "Delete").

**Note:** in order to set focus on an element that cannot natively receive focus (like a heading or the wrapper element), add the attribute `tabindex="-1"` to it.

description: The modal dialog container is not labeled.
recommendedFix:
Provide a [label using one of the following methods](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/820#heading-labelling). All of these solutions are acceptable, but some may be easier to implement than others depending on the content within the modal dialog.

1. Add a heading (preferably an `<h1>`, but `<h2>` is acceptable), then associate it with the modal dialog wrapper by giving that heading a unique `id` and referencing it with an `aria-labelledby` attribute on the wrapper element (the element with `role="dialog"` and `aria-modal="true"`).
  * If a heading describing the contents of the modal dialog already exists, you can use that heading instead.
  * This heading is most helpful when it is visible for all users, but for strict WCAG conformance it can be made visible only to screen reader users instead.
1. Alternatively, add an `aria-label` attribute to the wrapper element (the element with `role="dialog"` and `aria-modal="true"`) describing the purpose of the modal dialog.

description: Keyboard users are able to focus on elements outside of this modal dialog while it is open.
recommendedFix: Do not allow Tab or Shift + Tab to move focus outside of a modal dialog. See the [code sample provided in the related Knowledge Base article](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/820#heading-trapping-keyboard-focus) for additional details.

description: Closing this modal dialog does not return the user to the element that opened it.
recommendedFix:
When this modal dialog closes, return focus to the element that triggered this modal dialog to open.

If this element is no longer available on the page, then focus should be moved to another element as close as possible to where that element was.

If this modal dialog was opened automatically when the page loaded, then move focus on to the `<body>` element.

recommendedFix: Label the close button for screen reader users.  Depending on the situation, some options include:  * Add [screen reader only text](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/262) of “close” inside of the `

description: This modal dialog is missing necessary ARIA attributes.
recommendedFix: Ensure the attributes `role="dialog"` and `aria-modal="true"` are present on the wrapper element of this modal dialog. Do not [add these attributes](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/820#heading--do-not-dynamically-add-these-attributes-while-a-users-focus-is-inside) dynamically after the user's focus has been moved to it or into it.

description: This is a button, but it is not marked up as such; screen readers will not identify it as actionable and it will not be usable by keyboard users.
recommendedFix:
Preferably, buttons should be marked up as semantic HTML `<button>` elements.

Less preferably, ensure that custom button elements include `role="button”` and `tabindex=“0”`, and have the appropriate scripting in place so that the element can be selected by keyboard users using the `Enter` key and `Space` key, and by mouse click.

description: Focus indicators for actionable elements must be present and meet contrast requirements.
recommendedFix:
A focus indicator must always be visible and have at least 3:1 contrast.

It is best to intentionally style the focus indicator for all links, buttons, fields, etc. We encourage you to change the shape somehow (add a border, box, underline, etc.) as well as choose a color that has sufficient contrast with either the background of the page (if placed outside of the element) or the element itself (if placed inside of the element).

description: Tables with visible column and/or row headers must be properly indicated to screen readers.
recommendedFix:
Ensure that text serving as the header for each column is marked up in a `<th scope=“col”>`. 

Ensure that text serving as the header for each row (if present) is wrapped in a `<th scope=“row”>`. Often this text is the first cell in each row, [but not always](https://hub.accessible360.com/kb/articles/29#heading-not-always-the-first-row-or-first-column).

affectedItem: "Custom fields" > "Invoice Item Details" and "Invoice Item Details" > lists
description: This content is marked up as a table; however it is semantically a list.
recommendedFix: Remove the `<table>` wrapping this content and mark this up as a standard HTML list as appropriate to the content.

additionalElements: "Custom fields" > "Invoice Item Details" and "Invoice Item Custom Fields"
description: Text that functions as a heading should be marked up as such.
recommendedFix:
Mark this text up as a heading.

Headings provide structure for screen reader users. When marking text up as a heading, verify that the page maintains a logical outline structure. For example; 

- Each page needs a single `<h1>` heading that describes the main purpose of the page.
- An `<h2>` should head each major section of the page.
- Subsequent heading levels (`<h3>` through `<h6>`) should be related to a parent `<h2>` and should not skip heading levels.

description: Undersized targets cause problems for some users.
recommendedFix:
Users with reduced fine motor skills may have difficulty selecting smaller target areas, or may accidentally select another target nearby.  

Ensure pointer targets are large enough to allow for a 24 px square to be placed inside of it.

If this is not possible, provide sufficient space between targets: 

* at least 24 px between the center point of the undersized target and the center point of any other undersized target
* at least 12 px between the center point of the undersized target and the edge of a sufficiently sized target.

See the [WCAG Guideline](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/target-size-minimum.html) for more guidance on target size and spacing.

description: Elements that are marked up as links but function as buttons can cause confusion for screen reader users.
recommendedFix:
Mark each element up as a `<button>`. 

Alternatively, ensure that custom button elements include `role="button”` and `tabindex=“0”`, and have the appropriate scripting in place so that the element can be selected by keyboard users using the `Enter` key and `Space` key, and by mouse click.
